https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c9v4.text: Image source, BBC Mundo Image caption, Deivi (left) with Winder and their father Deivid By Agustina Latourrette BBC Mundo Published 14 August 2026 "The earthquake is haunting me," Deivi DelfÃ­n says. The 15-year-old feels like he and his brother, Winder, have been chased by tremors these past few months, having lived through two that struck with devastating effect in Venezuela, only to get caught up in another this week after moving to Colombia. He tells the BBC that he and his brother, 17, no longer felt like children, having witnessed corpses damaged beyond recognition. After their home in La Guaira - the area of Venezuela hardest hit by the twin quakes on 24 June - was reduced to a pile of rubble, killing three family members including their mother, they moved to Cali, Colombia, where their father works, on Friday. Three days later, they felt the ground shake again. 'My world came crashing down' Back at the end of June, the two teenagers had gone to the beach on Venezuela's Caribbean coastline. Winder wanted to take their 10-year-old brother MoissÃ©s, but he was grounded. "I kept insisting but my mum just wouldn't budge," he says. As they were heading home on the evening of the 24th, earthquakes of magnitude 7.2 and 7.5 struck just 39 seconds apart. The brothers hugged and shut their eyes. When they reopened them, everything was covered in dust and debris. When they arrived home, they saw the 12-storey apartment building had collapsed, trapping their mother Yusmani, grandmother Carmen and brother under a mountain of concrete. "My world came crashing down," Winder says. The earthquakes killed more than 6,300 people, according to the Venezuelan government. There is still no clear official figure for the number of people missing. Winder and Deivi joined rescue efforts, but for three days had nowhere to sleep and nothing to eat. Their father, Deivid, who was in Colombia at the time, was unable to find them for three days after returning to Venezuela. When he eventually found his sons, they began a search for their family members that would last nearly a month. Image source, Getty Images One month after earthquakes, Venezuelans still search for loved ones and answers Published 24 July Earthquake is devastating blow to Venezuela at time of uncertainty Published 26 June Families search for earthquake survivors in one of Venezuela's hardest hit areas Published 1 July 'I didn't feel like a child anymore' Deivid knew that climbing into the rubble would put his sons at risk, but they would not be deterred from searching for their missing family members. As they were still teenagers, they were better able to squeeze through narrow spaces, crawling between concrete slabs lit only by a handheld torch or mobile phone so they could tell rescuers where to dig. "By that point, I didn't feel like a child anymore," Deivi recalls . Gradually, they unearthed fragments of their family life - MoissÃ©s's shorts, Yusmani's Bible, and an unfinished shopping list - a sign they were getting closer to what had once been their home. The following day, Deivi spotted a piece of fabric in the rubble and recognised it as his grandmother's floral skirt. Soon after, firefighters confirmed they had found a woman's body. Image source, BBC Mundo Image caption, Deivi says he does not feel like a child anymore after weeks of searching for his missing family Winder was the first to recognise his mother's body. A plastic bag she had been using to dye her hair when they had left for the beach was still on her head. He got as close to her as he could and stayed with her for a few moments. They still could not immediately recover her body as it had been pinned down by a concrete slab. It was only while they were removing it that they found MoissÃ©s. The little boy was still holding onto his mother. At the sight of his son, Deivid collapsed. "When his little head fell into my hands... I broke down," he says. Image source, BBC Mundo Image caption, Winder was the first to see his mother in the rubble of their collapsed apartment 'We've been through this before' After laying their family members to rest, the brothers went to live with their father in a modest, working-class neighbourhood of low-rise houses in the north-eastern outskirts of Cali, Colombia. They say they hope for a life filled with hard work and study, so their mother would be proud. But having only just settled into their new home, they felt a sensation on Monday that was all too familiar. Colombia had been hit by its strongest earthquake this century - a magnitude 7.4, which killed several hundred across the country, with many more still missing. Cali was, once again, among the hardest-hit areas. Image source, DelfÃ­n family Image caption, MoissÃ©s was found still holding his mother Yusmani's (left) hand Deivi, who was asleep when the tremor began, says that he thought he was dreaming when the movement was gentle. But when it intensified, he got out of bed and ran downstairs. His brother did the same. Outside, they grabbed hold of a metal gate and waited for the shaking to stop. Their father had been out on the street at the time. As soon as he felt the tremor, he thought of his sons and ran back to the house - but when he arrived, they were nowhere to be seen. A neighbour told him she had seen them leave and he kept searching through the streets until he found them outside the barbershop where he worked. His sons tried to reassure him, saying: "Dad, stay calm. We've been through this before." https://telex.hu/techtud/2026/09/01/vite.text: Menü Kereső Megtette a kormány az első lépést, hogy újra működhessen a Planetárium Techtud Molnár Zoltán Állítsd be a Telexet megbízható forrásnak! Beállítom Kedden törvényjavaslatot nyújtott be a kormány az Országgyűlésnek, amivel rendezné több közterület sorsát, a Népligetben lévő Planetáriumét is. A törvényjavaslat a Planetárium hasznosítása és felújítása érdekében az ingatlan vagyonkezelői jogát a Tudományos Ismeretterjesztő Társulattól a Magyar Műszaki és Közlekedési Múzeumnak adja át. Így fogalmaznak a Vitézy Dávid közlekedési és beruházási miniszter által szignózott javaslatban: „A törvény biztosítja a Budapesti Planetáriumnak mint a hazai csillagászati és természettudományos ismeretterjesztés meghatározó intézményének megújítása és ismételt látogathatóvá tétele érdekében a hosszú távú muzeális és közösségi hasznosítását.” A javaslat nemcsak az épületre terjed ki, hanem többek közt „a Planetárium rendeltetésszerű működéséhez és eredeti építészeti, valamint kulturális, tudományos ismeretterjesztő funkciójához tartozó csillagvetítő, annak tartozékai és kapcsolódó technológiai berendezései” is ide tartoznak. A vagyonkezelői jog létesítése ingyen történik meg, a javaslat pedig rendelkezik a felújítás és bontás felelősségi köreiről is. Tanács Zoltán tudományos és technológiai miniszter még július 24-én látogatta meg az évek óta zárva tartó Planetáriumot. A Tudományos Ismeretterjesztő Társaság (TIT) 1977-ben nyitotta meg a Népligetben álló Planetáriumot, aminek 23 méter átmérőjű kupolájában egyszerre 400 nézőnek tudtak csillagászati ismeretterjesztő vetítéseket, és később más műsorokat is tartani. Az épület 2016-ban beázott, emiatt 2017-ben bezárták, és azóta sem nyitott ki. Tanács látogatásakor azt ígérte, megvizsgálják a többmilliárdos felújítás és újranyitás lehetőségét. Augusztus 22-én Tanács közölte , elkezdődött a kormányzati előterjesztés elkészítése a Planetárium ügyében. A miniszter azt írta, hogy három lehetséges fejlesztési irányt vizsgálnak: a 2027-es ideiglenes újranyitást, egy teljes, modern felújítást, illetve egy Tudományos és Technológiai Élményközpont létesítését a Planetárium köré. „Az ideiglenes megnyitás pár hónapig működhetne és néhány százmillió forintból megoldható” – írta Tanács, aki szerint a Planetárium teljes felújítása 2-3 évet venne igénybe a beszerzésekkel és a kiállításokkal együtt, becsült költsége pedig 15–20 milliárd forintos tartományban mozog. https://www.theguardian.com/australia-ne.text: Andrew Hastie leaving the federal court in 2022 after giving evidence as part of the Ben Roberts-Smith defamation trial. Photograph: Bianca de Marchi/AAP View image in fullscreen Andrew Hastie leaving the federal court in 2022 after giving evidence as part of the Ben Roberts-Smith defamation trial. Photograph: Bianca de Marchi/AAP Andrew Hastie Analysis ‘I don’t want to be here’: Andrew Hastie was a reluctant but ‘straightforward’ witness in the Ben Roberts-Smith defamation case Ben Doherty The Liberal MP and former SAS soldier is under attack from One Nation after complying with a subpoena to give evidence in the failed 2022 civil case Get our new political email , free app or daily news podcast Thu 10 Sep 2026 11.00 EDT Last modified on Thu 10 Sep 2026 11.02 EDT Share “I don’t dislike Mr Roberts-Smith at all. I pity Mr Roberts-Smith. I pity this whole process. I don’t want to be here.” Andrew Hastie was a reluctant witness in the Ben Roberts-Smith defamation case. Hastie appeared only under force of subpoena in 2022: compelled to attend court, obliged to swear an oath, and to tell “the whole truth and nothing but the truth”. His was an unhappy (of many) visit to the witness box. But it brought with it an additional scrutiny: he was, at the time of the case, not only a member of parliament, but the assistant minister for defence. Of the dozens of former SAS soldiers compelled to give evidence to the defamation case – many resentfully – Hastie was the only one named and photographed, the only one not afforded the protection of being a “sensitive witness”. In his judgment, Justice Anthony Besanko was approbative: “Mr Hastie was an honest and straightforward witness.” Three times, in fact, he characterised the former officer, now MP, as “straightforward” in his testimony. Andrew Hastie accuses Pauline Hanson and Barnaby Joyce of being ‘lying cowards’ over One Nation ‘traitor’ cartoon Read more Of Hastie’s former comrade who brought the defamation case – Victoria Cross recipient Ben Roberts-Smith – Besanko was equally forthright, but less complimentary. “[Roberts-Smith] was not an honest and reliable witness. “In each case, [his] motive for the lie is the realisation of guilt and a fear of the truth.” Sign up for Guardian Australia’s Politics, really newsletter here Now, for his testimony, Hastie has been referred to as a “gutless maggot” and a “traitor” in a cartoon posted online by Pauline Hanson’s One Nation party. Hanson, personally, said she would prefer to call Hastie a “wanker”. ‘Blooding’ Membership of “the regiment” – the SAS – is famously clandestine. Roberts-Smith and Hastie are perhaps its best-known former members. The pair’s service, while contemporaneous, was not tightly aligned. They are not close. Hastie, an officer, has written he remembers his first encounter with Roberts-Smith – the corporal ordering officer candidates into push-ups in a dead-of-night training exercise. He told the federal court there was a “widespread view” across the SAS that Roberts-Smith was a bully. Before the federal court, Hastie was asked to testify as to his recollection of an operation on a compound in a village known as Syachow in October 2012. It was his only operation in Afghanistan alongside Roberts-Smith. It was alleged before the federal court that on that mission Roberts-Smith ordered a subordinate soldier – known as Person 66 – to execute an unarmed prisoner in a so-called “blooding” incident. Hastie did not shy away from recounting details of the event in his testimony. Person 66, too, was subpoenaed to appear in court. He refused to answer a question about whether he’d been on operation in Afghanistan with Roberts-Smith as his patrol commander. “Person 66 objected to giving an answer to that question on the ground that it may tend to prove that he had committed the offence of the war crime of murder,” Besanko wrote in his judgment. On those grounds, Besanko could not find the allegation proved. Asked directly whether he ordered Person 66 to kill an unarmed prisoner, Roberts-Smith told the court: “I did not.” skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Politics, really Our political team brings you up to speed on the stories that really matter and what they mean for you after newsletter promotion Hastie told the court he once held Robert-Smith in “very high regard”. “I am no longer proud of Mr Roberts-Smith.” ‘Shoot him’ The alleged incident at Syahchow is one of the five war crimes murders with which Roberts-Smith has since been criminally charged. The statement of facts before the court reads that two PUCs – Persons Under Control – were hors de combat after an SAS raid on a compound. The two prisoners were handcuffed and blindfolded at the cessation of the raid. Jacqui Lambie calls Pauline Hanson an ‘angry little woman’ after One Nation cartoon calling Andrew Hastie a traitor Read more “Roberts-Smith cut the handcuffs from PUC 1 who was in front of Person 66, removed PUC 1’s blindfold and pushed him to the ground. PUC 1 fell backwards and put his hand in front of his face with his palms facing outwards. Roberts-Smith said ‘shoot him’. “Person 66 believed this to be an order from Roberts-Smith. Person 66 was two metres away from PUC 1. Person 66 paused for a moment and then shot PUC 1 two to three times in the chest, killing him.” The statement of facts states: “Person 66 has admitted their role in this incident.” Roberts-Smith’s case is now before the courts. He has consistently and vigorously denied the allegations against him. “For the past 10 years, my family and I have been subject to a campaign to convince Australians that I’ve acted improperly in my service in Afghanistan,” Roberts-Smith said in a statement after he was charged. “As I’ve always maintained, I categorically deny all of these allegations, and while I would’ve preferred these charges not be brought, I will be taking the opportunity to finally clear my name. “I have never run from a fight in my life. I will never give up, and I will always be in the fight.” Explore more on these topics Andrew Hastie Pauline Hanson Ben Roberts-Smith Australian politics One Nation analysis Share Reuse this content More on this story More on this story Albanese is under fire over a grants program that benefitted his local golf club. https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ck1w.text: Figure caption, Watch: Huge waves pummel northeast US as storm barrels through By Kwasi Gyamfi Asiedu Published 26 September 2026 Updated 3 hours ago Tens of millions of people across the north-eastern US have found themselves in the path of a powerful weekend storm bringing coastal flooding, power cuts, travel chaos and cancelled stadium events. The so-called nor'easter brought "dangerous coastal flooding and beach conditions, strong winds and heavy rainfall" to areas including New York City and Boston on Saturday, the US National Weather Service (NWS) said. States of emergency have been declared in New York and New Jersey, both of which faced a coastal deluge in some areas. Rain and strong winds were forecast from Virginia to Maine. In Brooklyn, New York City, a man was killed by a falling tree. Figure caption, BBC Weather presenter Helen Willetts look at the impacts of the powerful Nor'easter The nor'easter has caused widespread power cuts. More than 160,000 households, nearly all in the north-eastern US, have lost electricity, according to tracker PowerOutage. More than 2,400 flights were delayed and another 1,199 grounded on Saturday, according to FlightAware. A full moon was projected to worsen coastal flooding. Streets and homes were inundated with floodwater in the coastal New Jersey communities of Surf City and Manasquan on Saturday. Image source, Reuters Image caption, Surf City, New Jersey, was among coastal communities flooded NWS said in its alert: "Prepare immediately for significant inundation in low-lying areas near the shore, including roads underwater and impacts to homes and businesses." In New York, officials are warning of wind gusts of up to 55mph (86km/h) throughout the weekend, leading to downed trees and power lines. "Don't travel if you don't have to," NYC Mayor Zohran Mamdani told residents in a video message. "Do not drive or walk through floodwater." In the Boston area, the Red Sox moved the last game in their series against the Chicago Cubs to Sunday afternoon in Florida. Image source, Getty Images Image caption, Residents on kayaks in a Beach Haven West, New Jersey, neighbourhood A professional football match between Red Bull New York and St Louis City SC was also cancelled. The Global Citizen Festival concert in New York City's Central Park, which was to be headlined by Lauryn Hill, Wyclef Jean and John Legend, will not go ahead. Ed Sheeran's Boston concert was also among events called off due to the weather. Sheeran's concert at the Gillette Stadium in the Boston area was cancelled for safety reasons, the venue said. https://www.politico.eu/article/britains.text: LONDON — Britain's intelligence agency GCHQ cannot account for the whereabouts of thousands of storage devices which could contain sensitive material, according to an official watchdog. A report by the Investigatory Powers Commissioner (IPCO) — which polices how Britain’s intelligence agencies use their spying powers — on Thursday found that a significant number of devices including USB sticks, hard drives and memory cards are unaccounted for. Brian Leveson, the Investigatory Powers Commissioner, said that GCHQ “still cannot tell me what has happened to removable media that may hold sensitive data, years after I first raised it with them.” Advertisement Advertisement He noted that the devices “may contain IPA-related data” — which has a high level of sensitivity. IPA-related data refers to information collected or held under the Investigatory Powers Act 2016. That could include intercepted communications such as emails, texts and telephone calls, as well as information extracted from people’s computers or phones. The report added that GCHQ currently estimates the number of devices “to be in the thousands” and is currently undergoing work so it can report how many of the devices have been confirmed as lost. “We remain very concerned about this issue and are disappointed with the time it has taken GCHQ to investigate,” the report notes. Last year IPCO disclosed that GCHQ and fellow intelligence agency MI5 had been unable to locate considerable numbers of storage devices, some of which potentially containing information classified as "TOP SECRET." A GCHQ spokesperson said: “As IPCO have reported, our management system for removable media was previously not sufficiently robust to effectively track the items that were registered for use. IPCO are right to note the flaws in the data the system produced, and we have taken action against all their recommendations. "We recognise the importance of security of removable media in our systems, and have a range of measures to mitigate the risks posed by these items. The findings in the report have been addressed comprehensively and all necessary steps to correct this issue have been taken." Advertisement Advertisement
